name: Epson Home Cinema 2350
summary: A bright, colorful 3LCD 4K PRO-UHD projector with Android TV built in and a 1.6x zoom, held back by lamp upkeep and no optical lens shift.
verdict:
The Epson Home Cinema 2350 is the easy way into 4K-class projection for a living room. It uses Epson's **4K PRO-UHD pixel shifting** (1080p 3LCD chips shifted to put 4K detail on screen, see [how pixel shifting works](/glossary/pixel-shifting/)) and is rated at **2,800 ISO lumens** for both white and color brightness, which is where 3LCD beats single-chip DLP rivals.

Show the maths for a 120" 16:9 screen: the image is 104.6" (8.7 ft) wide and covers about 42.7 sq ft. The **1.32–2.15 throw ratio** puts the lens between **11.5 ft and 18.7 ft** from the screen (width x throw ratio; check your room with our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/)). Brightness works out to about 66 lumens per sq ft, or roughly 66 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses. That is plenty for a dark room and enough for evening viewing with some lights on.

The catch is placement. With no optical lens shift, the lens has to sit close to the screen's horizontal center line, so a shelf or ceiling mount must be planned rather than improvised. Black levels are fine for the price but not in the class of the [Epson Home Cinema 5050UB](/gear/epson-home-cinema-5050ub/). If you want built-in streaming and big, saturated color without spending laser money, it is one of the safest picks in our [best budget projector guide](/best-budget-home-theater-projector/).

faqs.a: No. It uses 1080p 3LCD chips and pixel shifting (4K PRO-UHD) to place 4K-level detail on screen. It accepts native 4K HDR signals, and at normal seating distances most viewers see a sharp, detailed image, but it is not a native 4K panel like a Sony SXRD projector.

faqs.q: How far back does the Epson 2350 need to be for a 120-inch screen?

faqs.q: Is the Epson 2350 good for gaming?
faqs.a: Yes for most players. Epson quotes input lag of about 20 ms, which feels responsive for console gaming. It does not offer the 240 Hz modes of some DLP gaming projectors, so competitive PC players may prefer an Optoma or BenQ gaming model.

name: Epson Home Cinema 880
summary: A cheap, very bright 1080p 3LCD projector for movie nights and bright rooms, with no zoom flexibility, no HDR and no built-in streaming.
verdict:
The Epson Home Cinema 880 is a brightness-first budget projector. It is native **1080p 3LCD** and rated at **3,300 ISO lumens** for both white and color light, a figure that is unusual at this price and the main reason to buy it.

Run the numbers. A 100" 16:9 screen covers about 29.7 sq ft, so the 880 delivers roughly 111 lumens per sq ft, or about 111 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses. At 120" (42.7 sq ft) that drops to about 77. Either way it has headroom to fight a lamp or two in the room, which matters more in a family room than a black-level spec does.

The trade-offs are real. There is no optical zoom (digital zoom only), so the screen size is fixed by how far away you place it; plan placement with our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/) before you buy a screen. It does not accept HDR or 4K, contrast is modest, and you will need a streaming stick. For a dark dedicated room, a 4K PRO-UHD model like the [Epson Home Cinema 2350](/gear/epson-home-cinema-2350/) is the better long-term buy. For a bright den on a tight budget, the 880 is hard to beat; see our [best budget projector guide](/best-budget-home-theater-projector/) for alternatives.

name: Epson Home Cinema 3800
summary: The most flexible mid-price Epson: 3,000 ISO lumens, 4K PRO-UHD, a 1.6x zoom and generous lens shift, with low input lag for gaming.
verdict:
The Epson Home Cinema 3800 is the step up from the [Epson Home Cinema 2350](/gear/epson-home-cinema-2350/) that fixes its biggest weakness: placement. It keeps **4K PRO-UHD** pixel shifting and adds **3,000 ISO lumens**, a **1.32–2.15 throw ratio** and lens shift of roughly **±60% vertical and ±24% horizontal**.

Here is what that means in a real room. On a 120" 16:9 screen (104.6" wide, 58.8" tall), the lens can sit anywhere from **11.5 ft to 18.7 ft** back. Sixty percent vertical shift moves the image up or down by about 35", so a rear shelf or a ceiling mount above the top of the screen both work without digital keystone, which softens the picture. Brightness lands at roughly 70 lumens per sq ft (about 70 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses), so HDR has some punch and a dimly lit room is no problem.

It is still a lamp projector, so budget for a replacement lamp, and black levels trail the [Epson Home Cinema 5050UB](/gear/epson-home-cinema-5050ub/) in a fully dark room. There is no built-in streaming. But for a mixed-use room where flexibility and brightness matter more than inky blacks, it is one of the best-value 4K-class picks in our [best 4K projector guide](/best-4k-projector-for-home-theater/). Check fit with our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/).

name: Epson Home Cinema 5050UB
summary: Epson's black-level specialist: 4K PRO-UHD with UltraBlack contrast, a motorized 2.1x zoom and huge lens shift, though it still uses a lamp.
verdict:
The Epson Home Cinema 5050UB is built for a dedicated, light-controlled room. Its headline is contrast: Epson rates it at **1,000,000:1 dynamic** with UltraBlack technology, and owners consistently report the deep, clean blacks that LCD-based rivals at this price struggle to match. Brightness is a healthy **2,600 ISO lumens**.

The lens is the other reason to buy it. A motorized **2.1x zoom (1.35–2.84 throw ratio)** places a 120" image from **11.8 ft to 24.8 ft** away. Lens shift is about **±96% vertical and ±47% horizontal**; on a 120" screen (58.8" tall) that is roughly 56" of vertical movement, enough for almost any ceiling or back-wall position. For brightness, 2,600 lumens over 42.7 sq ft is about 61 lumens per sq ft, roughly 61 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses. In a dark room that leaves room for HDR highlights or a bigger 135" screen.

The weaknesses are age and upkeep. It is a lamp projector, input lag is higher than newer gaming-focused models and HDMI is limited to 18 Gbps. If you want the same lens with laser and 4K/120, the [Epson Pro Cinema LS11000](/gear/epson-ls11000/) costs more. For pure dark-room value, it remains a reference point in our [best projector for home theater guide](/best-projector-for-home-theater/) and our [Epson projector review](/epson-projector-review/).

The Epson EpiqVision Ultra LS800 is the ultra short throw (UST) for bright rooms. It is rated at **4,000 ISO lumens** for white and color, among the highest of any consumer UST, and it uses a **laser** light source with **4K PRO-UHD** pixel shifting.

The throw ratio of about **0.16** is what lets it sit on a low cabinet against the wall. That headroom is why it holds up in a daytime living room where most projectors wash out.

name: BenQ TK710
summary: A 4K HDR laser projector with 3,200 ANSI lumens, 1.3x zoom, lens shift and fast gaming modes, the lamp-free successor to the HT2060 in our lineup.
verdict:
The BenQ TK710 replaces the 1080p HT2060 on our list and moves the formula up a class: **4K UHD** with HDR10 and HLG, a **laser light source** rated at **3,200 ANSI lumens** (see [ANSI lumens explained](/glossary/ansi-lumens/)), **1.3x zoom with lens shift**, and BenQ's claim of **95% Rec.709** color. BenQ quotes **16 ms input lag at 4K/60** and **4 ms at 1080p/240 Hz**, and eARC support lets it pass sound to a soundbar or receiver.

Run the brightness maths for your screen. On a 120" 16:9 screen (42.7 sq ft), 3,200 lumens is about **75 lumens per sq ft**, roughly 75 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses. At 135" (about 54 sq ft) it is still about 59, and at 150" (66.7 sq ft) about 48. That is comfortable for a dark room at any of those sizes and enough to keep a 100–120" image watchable with some lights on, especially on an ALR surface (see [how ALR screens work](/glossary/alr-screen/)).

The 1.3x zoom means the farthest throw is 1.3 times the closest, which gives you some freedom over where the mount goes, and lens shift avoids digital keystone, which softens a 4K image. The Amazon listing does not state the throw ratio, so plug BenQ's spec-sheet figure into our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/) before drilling.

Against the lamp-based [Epson Home Cinema 3800](/gear/epson-home-cinema-3800/), it trades a lamp for a laser in a similar price band. If the projector must sit close to the screen, the short-throw [BenQ TK710STi](/gear/benq-tk710sti/) is the variant to look at. For a bright, lamp-free 4K projector that also games well, it is a strong pick in our [best 4K projector guide](/best-4k-projector-for-home-theater/).

name: Optoma UHZ36
summary: Optoma's current 4K UHD laser home theater projector and the successor to the UHZ35 in our lineup, with HDR and Filmmaker Mode in a lower price band; check the lumen rating on Optoma's spec sheet.
verdict:
The Optoma UHZ36 replaces the UHZ35 on our list and keeps the recipe simple: a **4K UHD** DLP image, a **laser light source** with no lamps to replace, **HDR**, and **Filmmaker Mode**, which switches off motion smoothing and extra processing so films look as graded. It sits in a lower price band than the UHZ35 did, which makes it one of the more affordable laser 4K projectors from a major brand.

Amazon's listing is thin, with no lumen, throw or input-lag figures, so here is the maths that tells you whether 4K matters in your room. A 120" 16:9 screen is 104.6" wide. Spread 3,840 pixels across it and each is about **0.027"** wide, against 0.054" at 1080p. Normal vision resolves about one arcminute, so 1080p pixels merge beyond roughly **15.6 ft** from a 120" screen, while 4K holds detail down to about **7.8 ft**. If you sit 9–12 ft back, as most theaters do, the step to 4K is visible. Check your seats with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

For brightness, divide Optoma's rated lumens by your screen area: 42.7 sq ft at 120", 29.7 at 100". A result above about 50 on a 1.0-gain screen gives comfortable dark-room headroom. Then confirm placement with the [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/).

Compared with the lamp-based [Optoma UHD38x](/gear/optoma-uhd38x/), you trade its published 4,000-lumen, low-lag spec for laser longevity. Compared with the [BenQ TK710](/gear/benq-tk710/), it costs less, but the BenQ documents 3,200 lumens and lens shift. AWOL also claims anti-rainbow-effect processing, which matters if you see DLP color fringing, and native 24/48/50 fps playback for films and sports. UST rules still apply: a level cabinet and a perfectly flat, fixed-frame screen.

name: Dangbei N2 mini
summary: A tiny 1080p smart projector with licensed Netflix, a 190° tilt gimbal and full auto setup, the budget successor to the Dangbei N2 for dark bedrooms and dorms; the listing quotes no brightness figure.
verdict:
The Dangbei N2 mini replaces the N2 on our list and shrinks it further. It is a **native 1080p** smart projector on a built-in **190° tilt gimbal**, so it can aim at a wall, a screen or the ceiling, and it runs a Linux OS with **licensed Netflix**, YouTube and Prime Video. Setup is automatic: **auto focus, auto keystone, screen fit and obstacle avoidance**. Dangbei rates it at **under 27 dB**, quiet enough for a bedroom, and the power supply is built in, so there is one cable and no brick.

The catch is light, and the listing gives no brightness figure. Here is why that matters: image area grows with the square of the diagonal. Going from 60" (about 10.7 sq ft) to the maximum 120" (about 42.7 sq ft) spreads the same light over **four times** the area, so the picture is a quarter as bright. Projectors in this class are built for the dark, so plan on 60–80" in a blacked-out room and treat 120" as an occasional treat. Check sizes with our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/).

Auto keystone is convenient, but digital correction rescales the image and softens 1080p detail, so the sharpest picture comes from placing it square to the wall. The built-in Dolby Audio speakers are fine for a bedroom; in a living room, a soundbar is a clear upgrade.

For a real home theater, step up to the [BenQ TH575](/gear/benq-th575/) for brightness or the [Anker Nebula Cosmos 4K SE](/gear/nebula-cosmos-4k-se/) for 4K in a portable body. As a cheap second screen for kids' rooms and dorms, it is easy to like; see our [best budget projector guide](/best-budget-home-theater-projector/).

name: Sony VPL-XW5000ES
summary: The most affordable native 4K SXRD laser projector from Sony, with excellent sharpness and processing, but a modest 2,000-lumen rating.
verdict:
The Sony VPL-XW5000ES is the entry point to **native 4K** projection. Instead of pixel shifting, it uses three 0.61-inch **SXRD** panels with a full 4096 x 2160 pixel grid, a **laser** light source and Sony's picture processing, which independent reviews praise for HDR tone mapping and motion handling.

Its weak point is light. Sony rates it at **2,000 lumens**. On a 120" 16:9 screen (42.7 sq ft), that is about 47 lumens per sq ft, roughly 47 foot-lamberts on a 1.0-gain screen before calibration losses. Calibrated output will be lower, so for HDR in a dark room, stick to 100–120" or use a slightly higher-gain screen. At 100" (29.7 sq ft) the figure is about 67. Its **1.38–2.21 throw ratio** (1.6x zoom) places a 120" image **12.0–19.3 ft** away; check with our [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/).

Against Epson's pixel-shifting laser models, such as the [Epson Pro Cinema LS11000](/gear/epson-ls11000/) and the newer [Epson Pro Cinema LS9000](/gear/epson-ls9000/), the Sony is sharper and more refined and in reviews, while the LS11000 is brighter (2,500 vs 2,000 lumens) with more lens range and a lower price. Against the [Valerion VisionMaster Max](/gear/valerion-visionmaster-max/), the Sony trades brightness and features for native resolution and a proven brand.
